claim: Distributed adaptive signal timing through local queue length feedback
mechanism: Each intersection adjusts its green time proportionally to its local queue length, with a small portion of adjustment influenced by immediate neighbors' states through limited communication
evidence: Myxomycetes adjust tube structures based on local flow conditions
Proportional control systems are stable for single intersections
Distributed systems can achieve global optimization through local interactions
assumptions: Queue length is the primary indicator of traffic demand
Local adjustments will propagate beneficial changes through the network
Proportional control without integral terms will prevent oscillation
Network topology is sufficiently connected for information propagation
expected_failure_modes: Oscillations between intersections when proportional gains are too high
Gridlock when neighboring intersections simultaneously increase green time for conflicting flows
Failure to adapt to sudden demand changes due to lack of integral control
novelty_rationale: Translates the myxomycete's flow-dependent structural modification into a traffic signal control system using only local measurements and neighbor communication, without requiring central coordination or predictive models
testability: Can be implemented in simulation with varying network topologies and traffic conditions, with metrics including average delay, convergence time, and oscillation frequency
falsifier: If the system fails to converge within 15 minutes under normal traffic conditions or exhibits persistent oscillations in signal timing across the network
